synopsis: Equivalence is a reasoned, evidenced claim that variant differences do not affect safety-relevant behavior; transferring validation to another machine model or sensor position is therefore a validation-domain extension requiring similarity and bridging evidence, not automatic inheritance [f12362, f189, f7569]. Evidence reuse is described as the biggest validation lever but the least documented, and neither quantified time savings nor a demonstrated reduction of large-family validation from years to months was found [f366, f261, f12361]. The recommended approach is common-core evidence plus explicit variant deltas, a parameterized family model validated at envelope corners, sensitivity analysis, and targeted bridge tests; whether the product range can actually be reduced to a few such families remains an experiment [f12359, f7573, f12365, f10887]. Machine-specific braking, dynamics, integration and sensing geometry limit transfer, while the reported MOSH regime requires independent verification of every type, model and serial number where braking characteristics differ [f3437, f11552, f5613]. As of the October 2026 basis described in the booklet, similarity arguments draw on ISO 19014-5, machine-specific ISO 21815-3 calculations and sampled physical verification, but no formal off-road regulatory acceptance, universal representative-machine rule, accepted transferred-brake-model test count or published off-road variant-transfer example was found [f2942, f2943, f6683, f6557, f7574]. Planning must also account for a 2027 sensor change invalidating parts of the reuse argument and for the unexamined requalification process following brake-component or control-software changes [f11912, f6612].

relations.note: Both define transfer as domain extension with bridging evidence, not inherited validation.
Both report no published case quantifying time saved through machine-model evidence reuse.
Both report no ISO rule qualifying a family through N representative machines.
Both require separate verification where machine braking characteristics differ; the latter names MOSH.
Both report no published off-road example of validated-model transfer between variants.
Both describe aerospace acceptance of service history with justified similarity; the latter names FAA guidance.
Variant-specific braking and integration explain why one family's success cannot establish another's coverage.
Changing blind-area geometry necessitates an equivalence argument across models and mounting heights.
Envelope-corner validation and bridge tests operationalize common-core evidence plus explicit variant deltas.
Lists the geometry, dynamics, sensing and environmental parameters needed in the proposed family model.
Sensitivity analysis specifies how to justify shared evidence for each variant transition.
Requires variant-level confirmation alongside equivalence-based coverage and targeted physical boundary tests.
The proposed family-model transfer method depends on demonstrating that meaningful parameterized families exist.
Specifies ISO 3450 brake data underlying machine-specific ISO 21815-3 CxS calculations.
Barrick's machine-specific observations substantiate the risk of dynamics and braking failing to generalize.
Sensor-change invalidation requires revisiting applicability boundaries and identifying necessary bridge tests.
Likely substantial test-reduction potential remains unquantified in safely removable physical tests.
The major reuse opportunity requires evidence-sharing architecture designed in from the start.
